title: Centralization and Admin Key Risk
text:
Many contracts, especially in their early life or in cross-chain
bridge systems, grant a privileged role — an owner, an admin, a small
set of validator or "keeper" keys — broad power over the system:
pausing it, upgrading its logic, approving withdrawals, or minting new
tokens. This is often a deliberate, reasonable design choice early on,
allowing a team to respond quickly to bugs before the system is
sufficiently battle-tested to decentralize further.

The risk isn't a flaw in the contract's code in the traditional sense —
the access control logic may be implemented correctly — it's that the
security of the entire system now depends entirely on how well those
privileged keys are protected outside the contract: how many people
hold them, how they're stored, and how many must cooperate to approve a
sensitive action. If too few keys are required, or those keys are
poorly secured, compromising them grants an attacker the same broad
power the legitimate admins had, bypassing the need to find any bug in
the contract logic at all.

This is typically assessed by examining how many independent signers a
sensitive action requires, whether that threshold is appropriate for
the value at risk, and whether the privileged role can be revoked,
time-locked, or further decentralized over time rather than remaining
a permanent single point of failure.

title: Flash Loan Attack Pattern
text:
A flash loan lets a borrower take out an uncollateralized loan of
essentially any size, on the condition that it's borrowed and fully
repaid within the same transaction — if repayment doesn't happen by the
end of that transaction, the entire transaction, loan included, reverts
as if it never occurred. This is a legitimate and useful DeFi primitive
on its own, used for things like arbitrage and collateral swaps.

It becomes an attack tool when combined with another underlying
weakness — most commonly price oracle manipulation, but also
governance vote manipulation or exploiting reentrancy — because it
removes the normal capital constraint an attacker would otherwise face.
Without a flash loan, manipulating a price or vote outcome meaningfully
might require capital the attacker doesn't have. With one, an attacker
can temporarily command a sum far larger than their actual holdings,
use it to distort some on-chain condition, exploit a victim contract
that trusts that condition, and repay the loan, all atomically and risk
-free if the attack succeeds, with the only cost on failure being gas.

The flash loan itself usually isn't the vulnerability — it's an
amplifier. The actual fix is closing whatever underlying weakness
(typically oracle design) the borrowed capital is being used to exploit.

title: Price Oracle Manipulation
text:
DeFi protocols frequently need an on-chain price for an asset — to
determine collateral value, calculate swap rates, or decide if a loan
is undercollateralized. Many protocols source this price directly from
another on-chain source, commonly the token reserve ratio of a
decentralized exchange liquidity pool, rather than from an external,
manipulation-resistant feed.

The vulnerability: a liquidity pool's reported price is just a function
of its current reserves, and reserves can be temporarily and
dramatically shifted within a single transaction by a large enough
trade — particularly when combined with a flash loan providing capital
far beyond what the attacker actually owns. An attacker can borrow a
huge sum, execute a trade that skews the pool's reserves and therefore
its reported price, interact with a victim protocol that reads that
distorted price as if it were legitimate, then reverse the trade and
repay the loan, all within the same atomic transaction.

Mitigation: use time-weighted average prices (TWAPs) computed over a
window rather than a single instantaneous reading, or use independent,
manipulation-resistant external oracle networks rather than deriving
price directly from a single pool's spot reserves.

title: BeautyChain (BEC) batchOverflow Exploit (April 2018)
text:
In April 2018, security firm PeckShield discovered an integer overflow
in the batchTransfer function of BeautyChain's BEC token contract, an
ERC20 token built to let one transaction send tokens to many addresses
at once. The function calculated the total amount needed as
`amount * receivers.length` and checked that the sender's balance
covered that total before crediting each receiver individually.

The attacker called batchTransfer with two receiver addresses and an
`amount` value chosen so that `amount * 2` overflowed the uint256 range
and wrapped around to a tiny number — small enough to pass the balance
check trivially. The balance check then passed using the wrapped,
overflowed total, while the contract still credited each individual
receiver the original, enormous `amount` value before the overflow.
The attacker effectively minted an arbitrary number of tokens for free.

The same batchOverflow pattern was found in several other ERC20
contracts using similar batch-transfer logic, not just BEC. Once
discovered, exchanges including OKEx halted BEC deposits and trading,
and the token's market value collapsed. The exploit is widely cited as
one of the clearest real-world demonstrations of why unchecked
arithmetic in token contracts is dangerous, and it predates Solidity
0.8.0's built-in overflow protection by several years.

title: bZx Flash Loan Attacks (February 2020)
text:
In February 2020, the bZx protocol suffered two separate attacks within
the same week, widely regarded as the first prominent real-world
demonstrations of flash loans being used as an attack tool, predating
the larger Harvest Finance incident by several months.

In the first, an attacker took out a large flash loan, used part of it
to open a heavily leveraged short position on bZx, and used another
part to manipulate the price on a decentralized exchange that bZx's
own protocol referenced for pricing that position — extracting
profit from the resulting mispricing before repaying the loan, all in
one transaction. The second attack, days later, used a similar
flash-loan-funded approach to manipulate a different price reference
and improperly inflate the value of collateral used to take out an
undercollateralized loan from the protocol.

Combined, the two incidents resulted in losses of several hundred
thousand dollars — modest by later DeFi standards, but significant at
the time as proof that flash loans could fund single-transaction
attacks at a scale attackers previously couldn't reach without large
amounts of their own capital, directly foreshadowing the much larger
oracle-manipulation exploits that followed across the rest of 2020.

title: Cross-Chain Replay After the Ethereum / Ethereum Classic Split (2016)
text:
When the Ethereum community executed the hard fork reversing the DAO
theft, it created two separate, parallel chains sharing the exact same
transaction history up to that point: Ethereum (the forked chain) and
Ethereum Classic (which continued the original, unforked history). At
the moment of the split, both chains had identical account balances and
used the same transaction signing format, with nothing in a signed
transaction identifying which chain it was meant for.

This meant a transaction signed and broadcast on one chain — say,
moving funds on Ethereum — was also a perfectly validly signed
transaction on Ethereum Classic, since the signature itself contained
no chain-specific information. Anyone could take a transaction they
observed on one chain and rebroadcast it on the other, and it would
execute again there exactly as if the user had authorized it
separately, potentially moving funds the user never intended to touch
on that second chain at all.

This incident is the direct reason EIP-155 was introduced shortly
after, adding a chain ID into the transaction signing format so a
signed transaction is cryptographically bound to one specific chain and
can never be validly replayed on another — a fix that's now a
fundamental, invisible part of how every Ethereum transaction is
signed.

title: GovernMental Ponzi Scheme Gas Limit Lockup (2015)
text:
GovernMental was an early (2015) Ethereum Ponzi-style contract: players
sent ETH to join, and the payout structure was designed so that the
single last player to join before activity stopped for a long enough
period would receive the entire accumulated pot, paid out via a
function that looped through the full list of all participants to
settle balances.

As the game grew popular, the participant list grew alongside it. The
payout function's gas cost scaled directly with that list's length, and
eventually the list grew long enough that fully executing the payout
loop required more gas than a single Ethereum block could provide at
the time. The function became permanently uncallable — not failing
occasionally, but unable to ever complete again under any circumstance,
since no block could fit it — leaving roughly 1,100 ETH locked in the
contract with no built-in alternative withdrawal path.

This incident is one of the earliest and most frequently cited
real-world demonstrations of why "loop over all users and pay everyone
in one transaction" is a fundamentally unsafe pattern at scale, and it
helped popularize the pull-over-push withdrawal pattern that's now
considered standard practice.

title: Harvest Finance Oracle Manipulation (October 2020)
text:
In October 2020, an attacker used a large flash loan to manipulate the
reserve ratio of a Curve stablecoin liquidity pool that Harvest
Finance's yield vaults relied on for pricing. Harvest's vaults
calculated the value of deposited assets directly from that pool's
instantaneous reserves rather than a time-weighted average.

The attacker executed a large swap to distort the pool's reported
price, deposited into Harvest's vault at the artificially favorable
price this created, reversed the swap to restore the pool to roughly
its original state, then withdrew from the vault — repeating this cycle
multiple times within the same block. Each cycle extracted real value
from the vault's other depositors, who were unaware their pooled funds
were being mispriced.

The attack drained roughly $24 million from Harvest's vaults in under
ten minutes, all within a sequence of atomic, flash-loan-funded
transactions. It's one of the most cited early examples of price oracle
manipulation as a practical, repeatable DeFi attack rather than a
theoretical concern, and accelerated the industry's shift toward
TWAP-based and external oracle pricing.

title: King of the Ether Throne Refund Bug (2016)
text:
King of the Ether Throne was an early Ethereum game, launched in 2016,
where a player became "King" by sending more ETH than the current
king's claim price. The contract was meant to refund the deposed king
their claim price automatically when a new player took the throne.

The refund was sent using a low-level send-style call without checking
whether it succeeded. If the deposed king was a contract address rather
than a regular wallet — for instance, one whose fallback function did
more work than the gas stipend allowed, or simply rejected incoming
ETH — the refund call failed silently. Because the return value was
never checked, the contract had no way of knowing the refund hadn't
gone through, and the throne still changed hands to the new king as if
everything had completed normally. The deposed king's funds were left
stranded in the contract with no built-in way to reclaim them.

This case is widely cited in smart contract security literature (it
appears, for example, in academic surveys of Ethereum contract attacks)
as one of the clearest illustrations of why ignoring a low-level call's
return value isn't just a theoretical concern — it directly cost real
users real ETH in a live, publicly used contract, well before
"unchecked call return value" was a commonly known pattern to test for.

title: MEV and Sandwich Attacks in DeFi
text:
Rather than one named incident, front-running in modern DeFi is best
understood through MEV (maximal extractable value) — the broad,
continuously occurring practice of reordering, inserting, or censoring
transactions for profit. This was formally documented in the 2019
academic paper "Flash Boys 2.0" by Daian et al., which empirically
measured front-running and related extraction happening across
Ethereum in real time, drawing a direct parallel to high-frequency
trading front-running in traditional finance.

The most common pattern on decentralized exchanges is the sandwich
attack: a bot detects a pending trade that will move a token's price
(for example, a large swap on an automated market maker), submits its
own buy order just before it with a higher gas price, lets the victim's
trade execute at the now worse price, then immediately sells right
after at the inflated price — profiting from the victim's trade without
ever taking on directional market risk.

Unlike a one-time exploit, MEV extraction is ongoing and measured in
the billions of dollars cumulatively, and entire infrastructure (such
as Flashbots) has been built specifically around managing how it
happens rather than eliminating it outright.

title: Parity Wallet Library Self-Destruct (November 2017)
text:
In November 2017, several months after the July multisig theft from
the same project, a second and unrelated bug in Parity's wallet system
caused a much larger amount of ETH to become permanently frozen rather
than stolen.

Parity's multisig wallets used delegatecall to a shared library
contract for their core logic, to save deployment cost across many
wallets. That library contract had its own initialization function,
left callable by anyone due to the same class of missing access-control
bug as the July incident — and, critically, the library contract also
contained a function that could trigger `selfdestruct`.

A user (reportedly experimenting, not maliciously) called the
library's uninitialized init function, became its "owner," and then
called the function that triggered selfdestruct on it. Because every
multisig wallet relied on that one library via delegatecall for all of
its logic, destroying the library instantly and permanently disabled
every wallet that depended on it — freezing roughly 513,000 ETH (worth
over $150 million at the time) with no recovery mechanism, since the
library's code, not just its data, was gone.

This incident is the canonical real-world example of why a delegatecall
target's own vulnerabilities become the calling contract's
vulnerabilities too.

title: Parity Multisig Wallet Hack (July 2017)
text:
In July 2017, an attacker exploited a missing access control check in
Parity's multisig wallet contract. The wallet's initialization function
— meant to be called once, by the wallet's deployer, to set the initial
owners — had no check preventing it from being called again by anyone,
at any time, after deployment.

The attacker called this function on already-deployed, already-funded
multisig wallets and simply set themselves as the sole owner, then
withdrew the funds directly. Roughly 150,000 ETH (worth around $30
million at the time) was stolen across multiple wallets in a single
attack before the bug was understood and remaining vulnerable wallets
were rescued by white-hat actors.

This incident is one of the most cited real-world examples of a missing
access control check on an initialization function, and it directly
shaped the now-common pattern of guarding initializers with an
"already initialized" flag.

title: Ronin Bridge Validator Key Compromise (March 2022)
text:
Ronin was a sidechain built for the game Axie Infinity, secured by a
set of nine validator nodes; approving a withdrawal from the bridge
connecting Ronin back to Ethereum required signatures from five of
those nine validators. Four of the nine validators were run directly by
Sky Mavis, the company behind the game.

In March 2022, attackers compromised enough of these validator keys to
reach the five-signature threshold required for a fraudulent
withdrawal — including, notably, a fifth key obtained through a
compromised Sky Mavis system that had been granted emergency signing
authority during a period of high network load months earlier and was
never revoked afterward. With five valid signatures in hand, the
attackers approved withdrawals transferring approximately 173,600 ETH
and 25.5 million USDC — worth roughly $625 million at the time — out of
the bridge.

This remains one of the largest crypto exploits on record, and unlike
most incidents in this corpus, it involved no smart contract bug at
all — the contract's access control logic worked exactly as written.
The attack exploited weak key custody and an unrevoked emergency
permission, making it a frequently cited example of why contract-level
correctness alone doesn't guarantee security if the privileged keys
controlling it aren't equally well protected.

title: Rubixi Contract Ownership Takeover (2016)
text:
Rubixi was a Ponzi-style contract whose developer originally wrote and
named it DynamicPyramid, with a constructor function named to match —
standard practice at the time, since Solidity then required a
constructor to share the contract's exact name. The contract was later
renamed to Rubixi before launch, but the constructor function itself
was never renamed to match.

Because the function no longer matched the contract's new name, it was
no longer treated as a constructor at all — it became an ordinary
function, with default public visibility, callable by anyone at any
time rather than running automatically once at deployment. Multiple
users called this leftover function after launch to repeatedly reassign
themselves as the contract's "owner," a role with control over fee
collection, allowing attackers to redirect funds intended for other
participants to themselves.

This incident is widely cited in Solidity security writing as the
canonical example of why the old name-matching constructor convention
was fragile, and it's part of why the `constructor` keyword was
introduced shortly after to remove the renaming hazard entirely.

title: The DAO Hack (2016)
text:
In June 2016, an attacker exploited a reentrancy vulnerability in The
DAO, a decentralized venture fund on Ethereum that had raised roughly
$150 million worth of ETH from thousands of contributors. The DAO's
withdrawal function sent ETH to the caller via a low-level call before
updating the caller's internal balance record.

The attacker deployed a malicious contract whose fallback function
called back into the withdrawal function recursively, each time before
the balance had been decremented, repeatedly draining ETH within a
single transaction up to the call stack's depth limit. By the time the
exploit was halted, roughly 3.6 million ETH — about a third of The
DAO's holdings — had been redirected to the attacker's child DAO.

The fallout led the Ethereum community to execute a contentious hard
fork reversing the theft, which is the origin of the Ethereum /
Ethereum Classic split that persists today. The DAO hack is widely
cited as the first real-world demonstration of reentrancy as a
practical vulnerability, and directly motivated checks-effects-
interactions becoming a near-universal Solidity convention.

title: Block Timestamp as a Randomness Source — Attack Pattern
text:
Unlike reentrancy or the Parity incidents, timestamp dependence is best
understood as a recurring pattern across many small, often short-lived
gambling and lottery dApps rather than one landmark heist — these
contracts are numerous, individually low-value, and rarely receive the
same lasting public post-mortem treatment as a single large DeFi
exploit, but the pattern itself is extremely well established in
security literature and is one of the most consistently flagged issues
in automated Solidity analysis tools, including Slither.

The recurring shape of the bug: a lottery or game contract derives a
"random" winning value from block.timestamp (sometimes combined with
other on-chain values like block.difficulty, which carries the same
weakness). Because the entity producing the block has some control over
the timestamp within network-allowed bounds, a sufficiently motivated
participant who can also influence block production — or who simply
predicts the narrow range of plausible values — gains a real edge in
predicting or steering the outcome, breaking the fairness the contract
was designed around.

This is precisely why the security community converged on a strong,
near-universal rule: block.timestamp (and other miner/validator
influenced values) should never be treated as unpredictable for
anything where money is at stake.

title: tx.origin Phishing Attack Pattern
text:
Unlike reentrancy or access control, tx.origin misuse doesn't have one
famous named heist — its risk is best understood as an attack pattern,
widely taught via Ethernaut's "Telephone" challenge, which exists
specifically to demonstrate it.

The scenario: a wallet contract checks `tx.origin == owner` before
allowing a sensitive action like changing ownership. An attacker
deploys a malicious contract and convinces the owner to interact with
it — disguised as something innocuous, like a "claim your airdrop"
button. The malicious contract's function then calls the vulnerable
wallet's restricted function internally. Because the owner is still the
one who originated the outer transaction, tx.origin still equals
owner, the check passes, and the attacker's contract — now the
msg.sender — successfully executes the restricted action, such as
transferring ownership to itself.

The pattern is taken seriously industry-wide precisely because it's
easy to write and easy to overlook, not because of a single dramatic
loss event — most production audits flag any tx.origin authorization
check as an automatic finding regardless of whether it's been actively
exploited.

title: Uninitialized Storage Pointer — Attack Pattern
text:
Uninitialized storage pointers are documented directly in the Solidity
language's own official security considerations, rather than being
associated with one single famous theft — by the time DeFi-era
nine-figure exploits were happening, compiler-level protections
(introduced in 0.5.0) had already closed off most of the easy cases,
so this pattern is more historically significant as a language design
lesson than as a source of major recorded losses.

The general shape developers were warned about: a function declares a
local struct or array variable without assigning it to an existing
storage location, the compiler treats it as a storage-type reference
defaulting to slot 0, and any field written through that local variable
silently corrupts whatever real state variable lives in slot 0 of the
contract — commonly the first variable declared, which in many simple
contracts is the owner address.

This is a useful category to understand less for hunting it in modern,
compiler-protected contracts, and more for recognizing it instantly in
any older or unusual codebase still using pre-0.5.0 Solidity, where the
compiler offers no built-in safety net against it at all.

title: Function Default Visibility
text:
Prior to Solidity 0.4.22, a function with no explicit visibility
keyword defaulted to `public`, meaning any address could call it
directly — not just other functions within the same contract, and not
just an intended set of callers. A developer who simply forgot to mark
a sensitive function as `private` or `internal` would unknowingly leave
it open to anyone.

This was especially dangerous around constructor-like setup functions
in versions of Solidity where a constructor had to be named identically
to the contract itself rather than using the `constructor` keyword —
if the contract was ever renamed during development and the function
wasn't renamed to match, it silently stopped being treated as a
constructor at all and became an ordinary public function instead,
callable by anyone, at any time, not just once at deployment.

Solidity 0.4.22 introduced the `constructor` keyword specifically to
remove the name-matching fragility, and later versions require explicit
visibility on every function, eliminating the implicit-public default
entirely. The pattern remains relevant when reviewing any older,
pre-0.4.22 contract.

title: Integer Overflow and Underflow
text:
Solidity integers have a fixed bit width (uint8, uint256, etc.), and
prior to Solidity 0.8.0 arithmetic on them silently wrapped around on
overflow or underflow instead of raising an error. A uint8 holding 255
that gets incremented by 1 wraps to 0. A uint256 set to 0 that gets
decremented by 1 wraps to the maximum possible uint256 value, an
astronomically large number, instead of going negative or reverting.

This becomes a security issue whenever a contract uses unchecked
arithmetic on values that influence balances, allowances, or access
control — for example, subtracting a withdrawal amount from a balance
without first checking the balance is large enough lets an attacker
underflow their balance to a huge number and withdraw far more than
they ever deposited.

Before 0.8.0, the standard mitigation was OpenZeppelin's SafeMath
library, which wrapped arithmetic operations in functions that revert
on overflow/underflow instead of wrapping silently. As of Solidity
0.8.0, this checking is built into the language by default — addition,
subtraction, and multiplication all revert on overflow/underflow unless
the code is explicitly wrapped in an `unchecked { ... }` block, which a
developer would use deliberately when they've already proven the
overflow can't happen and want the gas savings.

title: Unchecked Call Return Value
text:
Low-level calls in Solidity — `.call()`, `.send()`, `.delegatecall()`,
`.staticcall()` — do not automatically revert the transaction if the
call fails. Instead, they return a boolean indicating success or
failure, leaving it entirely up to the calling code to check that value.
If the return value is ignored, a failed call is silently treated as
though nothing went wrong, and execution simply continues.

This differs from a normal Solidity function call or `.transfer()`
(prior to certain gas-related changes), which reverts automatically on
failure. With `.send()` in particular, a common but dangerous pattern
is writing `recipient.send(amount);` with no surrounding `if` check —
if the recipient is a contract that rejects the transfer (for example,
because its fallback function runs out of the limited gas stipend
`send` provides), the ETH is never delivered, no error is raised, and
the contract's internal state can end up inconsistent with what
actually happened on-chain.

The standard mitigation is to always check the return value explicitly
— `require(success, "transfer failed")` — or use the modern pattern of
`.call{value: amount}("")` combined with an explicit success check,
which is now generally preferred over `.send()`/`.transfer()` because
it doesn't impose a fixed, easily-outdated gas stipend.

title: Unprotected Functions and Access Control
text:
Access control vulnerabilities occur when a function that should only
be callable by a specific role — an owner, an admin, a particular
contract — is missing the check that enforces that restriction, or has
a check that's incorrect or bypassable. Common causes: a function meant
to be internal is left public, a modifier like `onlyOwner` is forgotten
on a sensitive function (changing ownership, withdrawing funds, pausing
the contract), or the check exists but compares against the wrong
value.

Standard mitigation is consistent use of access-control modifiers
(OpenZeppelin's `Ownable` or `AccessControl` contracts are the common
choice) applied to every state-changing function that should be
restricted, plus explicit tests confirming unauthorized callers revert.

title: Reentrancy
text:
Reentrancy occurs when a contract makes an external call to another
contract before finishing its own state updates, and that external call
gives the called party a chance to call back into the original contract
before the first invocation has completed. If the original function
relies on state that hasn't yet been updated, the re-entered call can
repeat actions — most commonly draining funds — multiple times against
state that should have blocked the second pass.

The classic trigger is sending Ether via a low-level call such as
`.call{value: ...}("")` to an address that turns out to be a contract
with a fallback or receive function written to immediately call back
into the original function, before that function has decremented the
caller's balance.

Standard mitigations: follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern
(update all state before making any external call), use a reentrancy
guard (a mutex-style modifier blocking re-entry while a function is
already executing), and be cautious relying on gas stipend limits from
`transfer`/`send` alone — gas costs aren't fixed long-term, and a
contract can still re-enter through other unprotected functions.

title: Uninitialized Storage Pointer
text:
Solidity variables of complex types (structs, arrays, mappings)
declared inside a function default to either `storage` or `memory`
depending on context and compiler version, and in older Solidity
versions this default wasn't always obvious or safe. A local variable
that's implicitly typed as `storage` but never explicitly assigned to a
specific existing storage variable doesn't point to "nothing" — storage
pointers default to slot 0 — so it silently points at whatever state
variable happens to occupy that contract's first storage slot,
frequently something critical like the owner address or a core balance
mapping.

Any write to that uninitialized pointer is then actually a write to
slot 0's real variable, not to a harmless throwaway value as the
developer likely intended — effectively giving an attacker, or even
ordinary contract logic, an unintended way to overwrite sensitive state
without any access-control check standing in the way, since the write
doesn't go through whatever function is supposed to guard that
variable.

Modern Solidity compilers (0.5.0 and later) catch most of these cases
at compile time and refuse to compile ambiguous storage references, but
the pattern remains relevant when analyzing or learning from older
contracts, and is still worth a static analyzer flagging explicitly
rather than relying solely on compiler version.

title: Delegatecall to Untrusted Callee
text:
`delegatecall` executes code from another contract in the context of
the calling contract — the called code runs using the caller's storage,
balance, and address, not its own. This is the mechanism behind
upgradeable proxy patterns and shared library contracts, but it means
the calling contract is fully trusting the callee to behave correctly,
since the callee can modify the caller's storage directly.

If the address being delegatecalled to is attacker-controlled, or if a
trusted library contract itself contains a bug, the consequences are
severe: an attacker can overwrite arbitrary storage slots in the
calling contract, including ownership variables, or — if the library
contract contains a `selfdestruct`, even one the original developers
considered safe — destroy the calling contract entirely, since
selfdestruct executed via delegatecall destroys the caller, not the
library.

Mitigation: only delegatecall to immutable, audited, trusted addresses,
and never to a library contract that itself contains a selfdestruct
reachable in any callable function.

title: Transaction Order Dependence
text:
All pending Ethereum transactions sit visibly in a public waiting area
called the mempool before a miner or validator includes them in a
block. Anyone watching the mempool can see a transaction's full
details — including, for example, that it's about to execute a
profitable trade or claim a reward — and submit their own transaction
offering a higher gas price (or use other ordering mechanisms) to get
included first, exploiting that visible information before the
original transaction confirms.

This is broadly called front-running, and it's an inherent property of
how public blockchains order transactions, not a bug specific to any
one contract. It becomes a contract-level vulnerability when contract
logic exposes value to whoever transacts first — a classic example is
a contract paying a reward to whoever submits the correct answer to a
puzzle first, where an attacker simply copies a pending correct answer
from the mempool and resubmits it with higher gas, stealing the reward
intended for the original solver.

Mitigations include commit-reveal schemes (submitting a hashed
commitment first, revealing the actual value later), and architectural
choices that don't expose exploitable ordering value in the first
place.

title: Authorization through tx.origin
text:
`tx.origin` returns the address that originally sent a transaction,
even if that transaction passed through several intermediate contract
calls. `msg.sender`, by contrast, returns whoever directly called the
current function — which could be the original wallet, or could be
another contract acting on its behalf.

Using `tx.origin` for authorization (`require(tx.origin == owner)`) is
unsafe because it can be bypassed via a phishing-style attack: if the
legitimate owner is tricked into interacting with a malicious contract
(for example, by calling one of its functions, or simply sending it a
transaction), that malicious contract can call into the target contract
on the owner's behalf. `tx.origin` still resolves to the real owner's
address — because they did, technically, originate the transaction —
so the check passes, even though the call didn't come directly from
the owner's intent.

This is a well-known enough pattern that it appears as a standard
teaching example in security training (notably Ethernaut's "Telephone"
challenge), rather than being tied to one specific incident. The fix is
simple: always use `msg.sender` for authorization checks, never
`tx.origin`.

title: Block Timestamp Dependence
text:
Solidity contracts can read `block.timestamp` as a source of "current
time." This value is set by whoever produces the block — historically
miners under proof-of-work, validators under proof-of-stake — and while
network rules constrain it to be reasonably close to real time and
greater than the previous block's timestamp, the block producer still
has some limited discretion over the exact value within that window.

This becomes a vulnerability when contract logic treats block.timestamp
as something an attacker can't influence at all, particularly when it's
used as a source of "randomness" (for example, deriving a winning
number from the timestamp's last few digits) or as a precise deadline
boundary where being off by even a small, producer-controlled margin
changes the outcome. A block producer who is also a participant in the
contract has a direct incentive to nudge the timestamp within their
allowed range to favor themselves.

Mitigation: never use block.timestamp as a randomness source (use a
verifiable randomness solution instead), and where timestamps are used
for deadlines, design the logic so a small, bounded manipulation window
doesn't materially change who benefits.

title: Missing Protection against Signature Replay Attacks
text:
Contracts sometimes accept an off-chain signed message as proof of
authorization instead of requiring an on-chain transaction directly —
for example, a user signs a message off-chain authorizing a transfer,
and a relayer submits it on their behalf, saving the user gas. The
contract verifies the signature came from the right address, then
executes the authorized action.

If the contract only checks that the signature is valid and doesn't
also track which signed messages have already been used, the exact
same valid signature can be submitted again — "replayed" — to trigger
the same authorized action a second time, a third time, or however
many times the attacker chooses, since a valid signature alone doesn't
expire or self-invalidate after first use.

This also applies across separate deployments and even separate
chains: a signature valid for one contract or one network can,
without proper safeguards, be replayed against a different deployment
of the same contract, or the same contract address on a different
chain. Mitigation: include a unique nonce in every signed message and
track used nonces on-chain, and include a chain ID and contract address
in the signed data itself so a signature is only ever valid in the
exact context it was created for.

title: Denial of Service via Block Gas Limit
text:
Every Ethereum block has a maximum amount of gas all its transactions
combined can consume. A function that loops over a data structure whose
size can grow without bound — most commonly an array of all users,
depositors, or participants — risks eventually requiring more gas to
execute fully than the block gas limit allows, once that structure
grows large enough.

Once that point is reached, the function becomes permanently
uncallable: any transaction invoking it will always exceed the gas
limit and revert, regardless of how much gas the caller is willing to
spend, because no single block can ever fit it. If that function was
the only path to, for example, distributing funds back to all
participants, those funds can become permanently stuck with no
remaining mechanism to retrieve them — the contract logic itself, not
just one transaction, is dead.

Mitigation: avoid unbounded loops over growable on-chain data entirely.
Use a "pull" pattern instead — let each user withdraw their own funds
individually in their own transaction — rather than a "push" pattern
that pays everyone out in a single loop.
